name: Ringo Corponation Lithocast Dead Drop Terminal
product_name: Ringo Corponation Lithocast Dead Drop Terminal
description:
The Lithocast Dead Drop Terminal is a hardened passive communications cache designed to be permanently or semi-permanently embedded in urban infrastructure — behind wall panels, inside building foundations, beneath pavement, or within utility conduit runs. Once installed, the unit stores encrypted messages in a local memory core and makes them available for retrieval by any authorized device that comes within 2 meters and transmits the correct handshake sequence over near-field low-power radio. The Terminal itself never broadcasts; it only responds to a valid handshake, and even then emits a signal measurable only at close range. To any passive monitoring sweep, an installed Lithocast Terminal is acoustically and electronically silent.

Ringo Corponation markets the Lithocast Terminal as infrastructure for 'resilient private communications networks in contested signal environments,' a description deliberately vague enough to satisfy regulatory review while accurately describing its primary use cases. The unit is encased in a composite housing rated to withstand 20 tons of compressive load, making it genuinely survivable when buried in concrete or installed behind structural walls. It draws power from a long-life isotopic microcell rated for fifteen years of standby operation with no external power connection required.

The terminal supports a message queue of up to 500 individual encrypted payloads, each with a configurable expiry timer. Messages past their expiry are overwritten with cryptographic noise. The device has no network connection, no GPS receiver, and no remote management interface — it is, by design, a completely isolated physical object. Finding one requires knowing where to look.

cultural_context: The Lithocast Terminal has given rise to a specific subculture of urban geography among operatives who maintain and use them: people who know the city not by its streets and landmarks but by the locations of silent, patient objects buried in its walls. Long-running networks of Lithocast Terminals — some installed over a decade ago, still active on their original microcells — have become a kind of hidden nervous system beneath certain districts. There are rumors of terminals whose original installers are dead, still holding messages that will never be retrieved, still waiting with fifteen-year patience for a handshake that will never come.
known_users: Corporate counter-intelligence units maintaining watch-point caches
story_hooks: A demolition crew breaking ground on a new Palladian Construction site finds a Lithocast Terminal in the rubble — and it still has 47 unread messages in its queue.
A character is given a handshake key and a district name, nothing more. Finding the terminal is the first part of the job.

Someone has been systematically locating and retrieving from Lithocast Terminals across the Undercroft — hitting drops that belong to completely unrelated networks, which means they have somehow acquired multiple handshake keys.
A terminal the team installed six months ago is still responding to the handshake ��� but the message queue now contains a message that none of the team members sent.

A dying contact presses a data chip into a character's hand: it contains the locations and handshake keys for a network of 23 Lithocast Terminals installed over the past decade. Whatever is stored in them is worth dying to protect.
